newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Fighting the trade in women's flesh.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Fighting the trade in women's flesh.

text.p: Sweden's European Commissioner Anita Gradin had no sooner moved into her new office in Brussels two years ago than she threw out the big brown leather sofa. The furniture was too male-oriented, she said at the time.

Out too went the easy chairs -- and in came more women to the higher echelons of power in the male-dominated Commission as Gradin, in the Swedish tradition, gave women half the jobs in her justice and home affairs cabinet.

After 40 years fighting for women's equality, abortion rights and better treatment for rape victims back home Gradin, now 63, took seriously her responsibility to introduce change as one of five new women to join the EU executive.
Only two women had ever before sat on the Commission in its almost 40-year history.
The diminutive Gradin -- known for her striking black hair, colourful dress against a sea of grey suits and explosive temper -- may have felt too small for the manly leather sofa.
But she soon leapt to a challenge not addressed by any man on the Commission -- putting the sex slave trade in women from eastern Europe firmly on the European Union's agenda.
CHANGING ATTITUDES TO VIOLENCE
When Gradin, a former Swedish equality and immigration minister, started campaigning against violence against women in the 1960s, conventional lack of wisdom said the victims were to blame.
"It was a time when you still had such conservative ideas around that the women were accused of bringing rape on themselves because they were wearing mini-skirts," she told Reuters.
Gradin explained she had experienced such attitudes when helping set up rape crisis centres and campaigning for better police treatment of victims in Sweden in the 1960s.

Almost 40 years later, she says no one could have any misconceptions about what is a modern kind of rape -- hundreds of thousands of eastern European women being trapped into prostitution in the 15-nation EU every year.

"It is about big power and big money. It seems that organised crime has found an area generating big money without real risks," she told a conference on women's rights at the European Parliament this week.

After the fall of the Iron Curtain took away economic security from many women, thousands were lured by criminals to the promise of a better life in the West as waitresses, dancers and hairdressers only to find themselves sold into prostitution.
Stripped of their papers after crossing the EU's borders, once discovered by the police they are usually treated as illegal immigrants rather than victims, and deported.

"In the sex market, they are deprived of their dignity, robbed of their earnings and exposed to violence and diseases. Without their documents, they risk being extradited without delay. And if so, they have no chance to (act as a) witness against their pimps or traffickers," Gradin said.
She says EU governments reacted with curiosity when she broached the issue in 1995 and then started to take stock of the situation in their own countries in time for a conference in Vienna last year.

"What I can see is an engagement," she said. "In December 1995 they were sort of curious. They said, 'Is it really that way?' Then they started to gather information about the situation in their own countries."
NO TO LEGALISING BROTHELS
While a solution to a complex problem is still not in sight, there is one option Gradin rules out -- mixing the issue with the debate on legalising prostitution.

She admits to being more perplexed than angry about recent remarks from one European deputy that her approach to the problem is too narrow and the illegal trade can only be achieved once brothels are legalised.
"This is a non-starter in a way because in most of our countries prostitution is legal," she said, adding that member states each had the right to set their own systems.
While waiting for a long-term solution to the trade in women, she is organising more collaboration between judges, lawyers and police throughout the EU on the issue.
She hopes Union will agree to bolster cooperation on criminal law during its current intergovernmental review of its treaties.
